details:
**Amaterasu hiding in a cave**
The Shinto sun goddess Amaterasu, angered by her brother's violence, shut herself in the cave Ama-no-Iwato and plunged the world into darkness. The other kami lured her out with laughter (provoked by the goddess Ame-no-Uzume's bawdy dance) and a mirror that showed her own radiant reflection. Japan's emperors claim descent from her.

**Flayed horse thrown at a loom**
The outrage that drove Amaterasu into the cave: the storm god Susano'o flayed a piebald horse and hurled it into her weaving hall, killing one of her weaving maidens. It is one of the most repeated clues for Japanese myth.

**Yamata no Orochi**
The eight-headed, eight-tailed serpent slain by the exiled Susano'o. It had eaten seven of an elderly couple's eight daughters, so Susano'o set out eight vats of strong sake, got the serpent drunk, and cut it to pieces with his ten-span sword (Totsuka no Tsurugi), then married the surviving daughter, Kushinada-hime.

**Kusanagi (the Grass-Cutter Sword)**
The sword Susano'o found inside one of Orochi's tails, which chipped his own blade. He gave it to Amaterasu, and it later became one of the imperial regalia. Its name, "grass-cutter," comes from a later legend in which the hero Yamato Takeru used it to mow down a burning field.

**Izanagi and Izanami**
The primordial husband-and-wife creator kami. Standing on the Floating Bridge of Heaven (Ame-no-ukihashi), they stirred the ocean with the jeweled spear Ame-no-nuboko, and brine dripping from its tip formed Onogoro, the first island. They built a home there around a great central pillar and gave birth to the islands of Japan and many kami.

**Izanami's death and the underworld Yomi**
Izanami died after giving birth to the fire god Kagutsuchi. Izanagi followed her to the underworld Yomi but saw her rotting, maggot-ridden body and fled, throwing objects including peaches at his pursuers. After he sealed the entrance with a boulder, she vowed to kill 1,000 people a day, and he answered that he would cause 1,500 to be born.

**Birth of Amaterasu, Tsukuyomi, and Susano'o**
When Izanagi purified himself in water after leaving Yomi, gods were born from his washing: Amaterasu from his left eye, the moon god Tsukuyomi from his right eye, and Susano'o from his nose.

**Jimmu**
The legendary first emperor of Japan, a descendant of Amaterasu, according to the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. On his campaign eastward to conquer the Yamato region he was guided by Yatagarasu, a three-legged crow, and he fought peoples later called Emishi, whose name is written with characters meaning "shrimp barbarians."

**Three Sacred Treasures**
The imperial regalia of Japan: the sword Kusanagi, the mirror Yata no Kagami (the mirror used to lure Amaterasu from the cave), and the jewel Yasakani no Magatama. Amaterasu gave them to her grandson Ninigi when he descended to rule the earth, and they passed to his great-grandson Jimmu. They are presented at the emperor's enthronement.

**Akitsushima (Dragonfly Island)**
A classical poetic name for Japan. In one story, Jimmu looked out over the land and said it resembled two dragonflies mating, forming a ring. In another, a dragonfly protected Emperor Yūryaku by eating an insect that bit his arm.

**Jimmu's ancestry and marriage**
Jimmu was the grandson of Hoori (Yamasachihiko), who lost his brother's borrowed fishhook and went to the palace of the sea god to find it, and Toyotama-hime, the sea god's daughter. Jimmu's empress was said to be the child of a woman impregnated by the god Ōmononushi, who had taken the form of a red arrow.

**Momotarō**
"Peach Boy," the hero of a famous Japanese folktale. He was found inside a giant peach floating down a river by an elderly couple, and he traveled to Onigashima, the island of ogres (oni), with a dog, a monkey, and a pheasant to defeat them.

**Inari**
The Shinto kami of rice, fertility, and prosperity, whose messengers are foxes (kitsune). In folklore, foxes grow more tails as they gain age and wisdom, up to nine. Inari shrines are known for their rows of red torii gates.

**Urashima Tarō**
A fisherman who saved a turtle and was rewarded with a stay at Ryūgū-jō, the undersea palace of the dragon god Ryūjin. When he returned home, about 300 years had passed. Ryūjin is also said to own two jewels that control the tides.

**Raijin and other folk tales**
Japanese parents tell children to cover their belly buttons during thunderstorms or the thunder god Raijin will eat their navels. Other tales say the jellyfish lost its bones as punishment for failing to bring Ryūjin a monkey's liver, and that the sea cucumber had its mouth slit for staying silent when the other sea creatures vowed to serve the descendants of the heavenly kami.
